body:
Different hazards require different immediate decisions

Earthquake, tsunami and cyclone risk management share the goals of saving lives, reducing damage and supporting recovery. Their operational differences arise from the physical nature of the hazard and the amount of warning time available.

An earthquake may begin with no usable advance notice. The first priority for a person indoors is protection from shaking and falling objects. A dangerous tsunami may follow certain undersea earthquakes, making rapid movement out of an exposed coastal area essential once it is safe to move. A tropical cyclone, by contrast, can often be monitored as it develops, permitting organised evacuation before landfall.

HazardImportant advance measureImmediate public protectionMajor recovery concern
EarthquakeSafer construction, retrofitting and household preparednessDrop, Cover and Hold On during shakingSafe buildings, utilities and aftershock-related risk
TsunamiWarning arrangements, coastal evacuation routes and reduced exposureLeave the threatened coast for higher ground or inlandInundated settlements, freshwater and fishing livelihoods
Cyclone and storm surgeForecast-based evacuation, shelters and resilient infrastructureFollow evacuation instructions and remain in safe shelterWind damage, coastal flooding, crops and marine livelihoods

Know which institution performs which function

Scientific monitoring and warnings are different from local disaster-response decisions. A national scientific institution may identify a hazard and publish a technical bulletin, while state and district authorities determine protective actions for particular communities.

  • National Centre for Seismology: Monitors earthquake activity and provides information about recorded seismic events.
  • INCOIS: Operates India's tsunami early-warning system and issues tsunami advisories.
  • India Meteorological Department: Monitors tropical cyclones and issues cyclone forecasts and meteorological warnings.
  • National Disaster Management Authority: Provides national disaster-risk-management guidance and a framework for preparedness and mitigation.
  • Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority: Supports disaster-risk reduction, planning, coordination, preparedness and recovery in Gujarat.
  • District and local authorities: Communicate local instructions, organise evacuation and shelters, coordinate relief and determine when affected areas can be safely re-entered.

The National Disaster Response Force and state disaster-response organisations provide trained response capacity when deployed. Their specialised role should not be confused with ordinary public precautions, which focus on reaching safety and following verified instructions.

A coastal earthquake can create a sequence of hazards

Consider a coastal settlement that experiences prolonged, strong earthquake shaking. The immediate danger is falling objects and structural damage. The correct initial action for a person indoors is to protect the head and neck and take cover during shaking. Once the shaking ends, the same person may need to evacuate rapidly inland or to higher ground because the earthquake could have generated a tsunami.

This example shows a cascading hazard: one event can create conditions for another. The possibility of a tsunami does not make it safe to run outside while a building is shaking, but it makes prompt coastal evacuation important immediately afterward.

Why Gujarat needs a multi-hazard approach

Gujarat's hazard profile includes the earthquake-prone Kutch region and a long Arabian Sea coastline exposed to cyclones, storm surge and possible tsunamis. The appropriate measures differ across locations and hazards.

A settlement in the Kutch region may need particular attention to earthquake-resistant construction. A low-lying fishing village may require cyclone shelters, safe evacuation routes and marine livelihood protection. A coastal location exposed to possible tsunami inundation may also require public knowledge of natural warning signs and rapid access to higher ground.

Risk maps, local building conditions and community characteristics must be considered together. One general precaution cannot replace hazard-specific preparation. Similarly, protecting lives during a disaster and restoring livelihoods afterward are both necessary parts of effective management.

Connections worth retaining

Seismic zones indicate regional earthquake hazard, not building safety. Tsunami alerts assess possible coastal consequences of water displacement, not the future occurrence of an earthquake. Cyclone warnings forecast developing weather hazards, but the eventual consequences also depend on the tide, coastline, rainfall and local vulnerability.

Across all 3 hazards, the most effective public measures are those taken in advance: safer buildings, reliable warnings where scientifically possible, accessible shelters or evacuation routes and community understanding of the right action at the right time.

Prelims focus

  • NCS: earthquake monitoring and reporting.
  • INCOIS: tsunami early-warning service.
  • IMD: cyclone monitoring, forecasting and warnings.
  • GSDMA: Gujarat-level disaster management, preparedness and recovery coordination.
  • Strong coastal earthquake shaking may require both immediate earthquake protection and subsequent tsunami evacuation.
  • Trap: The national agency issuing a hazard advisory is not necessarily the authority deciding when local residents may return.

[Sources: Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026, NCS responsibilities; Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Indian Tsunami Early Warning System and Standard Operating Procedure, institutional roles and public-action categories; India Meteorological Department, Cyclone Warning in India: Standard Operation Procedure, March 2021, Chapter 6; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, About Us, Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003, and Gujarat State Disaster Management Plan 2020–21, Volume 2, Chapters 1–3; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Plan, 2019, institutional framework and preparedness sections. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
title: Applying Hazard-Specific Preparedness and Institutional Roles in Gujarat
